summary:
Tula Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and the sources reviewed identify no regional deviation material enough to assess separately; the oblast is assessed at the national score. For a trans visitor the national position means that same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are both banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the 2023 Supreme Court designation of the "international LGBT movement" as extremist, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years. These provisions apply in Tula Oblast as in every other region.

Enforcement is documented at scale. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions — about 98 administrative and 3 criminal — for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia covering sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out this same legal position and records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office note assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them; it treats LGBT+ people as constituting a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the standard for UK asylum claims.

Official warnings to travellers are explicit. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement volume has grown in step with severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two preceding years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was recorded by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Lethal and coercive outcomes are on the record. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.

The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, with a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tula Oblast are subject to the same prohibitions as visitors on legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care: the 2023 law barring gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents removes the domestic route to changing a gender marker, and trans-specific healthcare is unavailable as a matter of law.

Russian residents account for the bulk of documented enforcement. Of the 101 extremism-related convictions recorded by Human Rights Watch as at 30 June 2025, roughly 98 were administrative and 3 criminal; 81 people were convicted in those 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, and at least 20 people faced criminal charges between January 2024 and June 2025.

Residents also face the domestic application of the propaganda statutes, which since the 2023 designation carry two to six years for participation and six to ten years for organising the designated movement, on top of administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days for a first propaganda offence and up to four years on repeat.

The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that the state is able but unwilling to protect openly LGBT+ people from societal discrimination that may amount to persecution.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tula Oblast-specific enforcement data — regional court records, oblast-level fines, detentions or raids under the propaganda or extremism provisions — appears in the sources reviewed. The absence of a regional deviation in this record reflects the scope of those sources rather than a verified finding that none exists.

Whether Tula Oblast authorities apply any additional local measures, or provide any local protective or support machinery for trans residents, is unresolved and not sourced here.

The sources reviewed do not establish regional hate-crime statistics, local police practice on document checks, or access to legal representation for trans detainees in the oblast. These remain unsourced.
